introduction_strategy.hook_hypothesis: Recent literature evaluates neural reasoning capabilities on discrete algorithmic puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme, arguing that looped recurrent networks or energy-based architectures learn foundational reasoning.
introduction_strategy.problem_gap_hypothesis: When measured on the same fixed budget of Sudoku-Extreme puzzles on identical hardware, the performance, cost, and reliability differences between internal LLM chain-of-thought, LLM code generation, and classical energy models remain uncharacterized.

related_work_strategy.overview: Investigate three specific methodology clusters to evaluate how discrete constraint problems are tackled: looped neural networks, classical energy-based models, and large language models using internal chain-of-thought versus programmatic tool generation.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.3 Direct LLM Reasoning vs. Programmatic Tool Synthesis
subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Identify studies comparing direct chain-of-thought solving against program-aided or code-generation approaches on strict combinatorial puzzles.
subsections.limitation_hypothesis: Frontier LLMs attempting direct chain-of-thought on strict puzzles suffer from cumulative attention drift, high token consumption, and catastrophic budget exhaustion.

Code generation versus direct inference discrete constraint reasoning LLMs
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: We explicitly benchmark direct solving against one-prompt Python solver synthesis using frontier Claude models on the exact same puzzle sample.

content_bullets: Contextualize the debate surrounding reasoning benchmarks like Sudoku-Extreme, where looped networks and classical energy models like CRAM (Hoover et al., 2026) claim rapid reasoning capabilities.

Formulate the comparative evaluation across three paradigms on 500 test puzzles on a single laptop CPU: (1) direct LLM solving with adaptive thinking, (2) LLM-synthesized Python backtracking solvers, and (3) an independent CPU re-implementation of CRAM.

Highlight empirical findings: direct LLM solving is expensive ($0.014-$0.426/puzzle), slow (105-166s median), and prone to token exhaustion or hallucinations; in contrast, LLM-generated Python solvers achieve 100% accuracy (4,500/4,500 runs) at 1.02-1.85 ms per puzzle with negligible one-time prompt costs.

Summarize CRAM replication results: CPU pseudolikelihood fits in 2.5 seconds and solves 496-497/500 puzzles, but a hand-set single-weight energy achieves identical accuracy (497/500), supporting the caveat that Sudoku-Extreme measures simple constraint satisfaction rather than deep reasoning.
Introduce the proliferation of combinatorial reasoning benchmarks (specifically sapientinc/sudoku-extreme) used to evaluate algorithmic capabilities in neural models.

Discuss the recent emergence of CRAM (Hoover et al., Nov 2026), which revives Hopfield-Tank energy formulations to solve Sudoku-Extreme rapidly, contrasting it with the practice of applying frontier LLMs directly via long chains-of-thought.

Define the core research gap: the absence of a controlled, hardware- and budget-normalized comparison between direct autoregressive reasoning, programmatic code synthesis, and classical energy minimization.

State Contribution 1: An empirical evaluation of direct chain-of-thought solving across Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5, revealing high latency, token limit failures, and subtle cell errors.

State Contribution 2: A demonstration that the same LLMs reliably synthesize standard-library Python backtracking solvers in one shot, achieving 100% accuracy across 4,500 evaluations at sub-2ms per-puzzle latency.

State Contribution 3: An independent, clean-room CPU re-implementation of CRAM (NumPy pseudolikelihood training and C focused Gibbs search), confirming 99.2%+ test accuracy and perfect constraint graph recovery.

State Contribution 4: Verification of Hoover et al.'s caution: a trivial hand-set energy with a single weight parameter matches learned energy accuracy, challenging the assertion that Sudoku performance reflects neural reasoning.

Detail the lineage of energy-based optimization and continuous Hopfield networks for combinatorial problems, leading to CRAM.
Differentiate our work: we provide a strict, budget-constrained CPU replication and baseline comparison.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.2 Direct Reasoning vs. Programmatic Problem Solving in LLMs

Discuss program synthesis, code execution, and programmatic backtracking as alternative pathways for deterministic logic.

subsections.subsection_title: 3.1 CRAM Formulation: Energy Grid and Pseudolikelihood Estimation
content_bullets: Formalize the CRAM discrete state representation over an 81 x 9 belief grid without exposing structural priors (opaque cell indices without row, column, or box coordinates).
Specify the energy function: negative entropy regularizer, pairwise 9x9 couplings across all cell pairs, and local bias vectors.
Define the objective function using pseudolikelihood maximization over the conditional probabilities of cell states, implemented in NumPy.
Describe the training protocol on the first 1,000 solved boards of the Sudoku-Extreme training split.

subsections.subsection_title: 3.2 Focused Gibbs Search and the Hand-Set Energy Baseline
content_bullets: Detail the focused Gibbs sampling algorithm implemented in C, operating with 4 parallel chains initialized from random boards on a single CPU core.
Define the stopping criteria and move budget (up to 10 million moves per puzzle, corresponding to ~6.3 seconds).
Specify the hand-set energy baseline: a single constant weight penalizing identical digits across Hopfield-Tank constraint cliques without any training or parameter fitting.

subsections.subsection_title: 3.3 LLM Solver Synthesis and Direct Evaluation Protocols
content_bullets: Define the direct-solving condition: prompt structure, adaptive thinking configuration, effort level set to high, and a maximum token budget of 32,000 output tokens.
Define the solver-synthesis condition: a single natural language prompt instructing the model to generate a self-contained Python solver using only the standard library.
Detail the test pipeline: generation of 3 independent solver scripts per model family (9 solvers total) and automated test execution across 500 benchmark puzzles.
Detail the test environment: single Apple M4 Pro laptop CPU, zero GPU utilization, total API expenditure capped at $3.75.
Describe the evaluation dataset: 500 test puzzles drawn from 5 seeded random pages of sapientinc/sudoku-extreme (median 26 clues per puzzle).

Clarify sample allocations: direct solving tested on subsets (Opus 5.5: 5 puzzles, Sonnet 5.5: 5 puzzles, Haiku 5.5: 10 puzzles) due to prohibitive costs; solver-writing and CRAM evaluated on the full 500-puzzle set.
Define evaluation metrics: puzzle solve rate, incorrect board stops, token exhaustion rate, API cost per puzzle, and wall-clock execution latency.

subsections.subsection_title: 4.2 Comparative Evaluation: Direct LLM vs. Synthesized Solvers vs. CRAM
content_bullets: Analyze direct LLM reasoning: Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 solve 3/5 puzzles each, failing on difficulty ratings 88 and 15 due to token limits at $0.426 and $0.250 per puzzle; Haiku 5.5 solves 3/10 puzzles with 2 outright hallucinated boards (74/81 and 78/81 correct).

Present synthesized Python solver results: all 9 generated solvers achieve perfect 500/500 accuracy (4,500/4,500 successful runs), with median latencies of 1.02-1.85 ms per puzzle and code generation costs under $0.06.
Contrast direct generation latency (105-166 seconds median) with programmatic execution (sub-2 milliseconds), highlighting an efficiency gap of five orders of magnitude.

subsections.subsection_title: 4.3 CRAM Replication, Constraint Graph Recovery, and Energy Ablation
content_bullets: Report CRAM re-implementation results across 3 random seeds: solves 496-497 out of 500 puzzles with 2.51-2.52 seconds CPU training time and 53.2-61.1 ms median latency.

Analyze failure modes: failures stem entirely from move budget exhaustion (~6.3s timeout); zero incorrect boards accepted; 10/10 solved on the LLM subset including puzzles where Opus and Sonnet timed out.
Demonstrate constraint recovery: the top-20 learned same-digit couplings for every opaque cell index match its exact 20 row, column, and box peers (peer recovery metric = 1.000).

Evaluate the hand-set energy baseline: achieves 497/500 solves with 42.8 ms median latency without training, demonstrating that learned weights provide no advantage over classical Hopfield-Tank penalty rules.
Synthesize the overarching conclusion: asking frontier LLMs to reason directly through complex discrete constraint puzzles is inefficient, costly, and error-prone.
Emphasize that programmatic synthesis via LLM code generation provides a robust, fast, and virtually cost-free solution for exact combinatorial reasoning.

Reiterate the validation of Hoover et al.'s replication: CRAM replicates effectively on a standard CPU, but the equivalence of hand-set energies underscores that Sudoku-Extreme evaluates constraint propagation rather than genuine algorithmic reasoning.
Acknowledge evaluation sample constraints for the direct-solving LLM condition necessitated by steep token expenditure.
Highlight reliance on CPU re-implementation rather than the original authors' proprietary GPU codebase.
Propose expanding comparative analyses to higher-order combinatorial domains where simple local energy structures cannot fully capture problem constraints.
